```{r}
# Set seed
set.seed(2)
```


## Problem 1

Suppose I recruit a sample of Bostonians and measure the duration of their daily commute (in minutes)
and their total cholesterol (in mg/dL).
The results below are from a regression of cholesterol on commute:

```{r}
# Parameter values
n <- 1e4
beta_0 <- 187
beta_1 <- 0
sigma <- 500

# Generate data
commute <- rnorm(n = n)
epsilon <- rnorm(n = n,
                 sd = sigma)
y <- beta_0 + beta_1 * commute + epsilon

# Run model
mod_01 <- lm(formula = y ~ commute)
summary(mod_01)
```


### Part (a)

(3 points)
Assuming the necessary assumptions are met,
what does 186.636 represent in real-world terms?
In other words, interpret the intercept for this study.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The expected (or average, or mean, or estimated; 1 point)
cholesterol (1 point) for a Bostonian whose commute is zero minutes long (1 point).
No points lost if you don't mention that we're talking about Bostonians specifically.

:::

### Part (b)

(6 points)
Assuming the necessary assumptions are met,
what does the value 6.998 represent in real-world terms?
In other words, intepret the slope for this study.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The expected (or average, or mean, or estimated; 1 point)
change (or increase; 1 point)
in cholesterol (1 point)
associated with a one-minute (1 point)
increase (or change; 1 point)
in commute duration (1 point).
No points lost if you used a causal interpretation;
that's not our focus right now.

Alternatively,
the expected (or average, or mean, or estimated; 1 point)
difference (1 point)
in total cholesterol (1 point)
between two populations of Bostonians
that differ (1 point) by one minute (1 point)
in the duration of their daily commute (1 point).

:::

### Part (c)

(2 points)
Assuming the necessary assumptions are met,
would you conclude that there's a linear relationship between commute duration
and total cholesterol among Bostonians?
Why or why not?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

No (1 point).
The p-value associated with `commute` is $0.167 > 0.05$ (1 point),
so we fail to reject the null hypothesis that the slope is zero.

:::

## Problem 2

```{r}
#| label: fig-qq
#| fig-cap: "Q-Q plot of the residuals for a simple linear regression."
# Generate non-normal random variables
z <- rgamma(n = n,
            shape = 2,
            rate = 0.1)
boxplot(z)
hist(z)
qqnorm(z)
qqline(z)
```


Suppose @fig-qq contains a Q-Q plot of the residuals for a simple linear regression.
For each assumption below, do the following:

- State whether @fig-qq is evidence for the validity
of the assumption in this data set, evidence against it,
or provides no information.
- If you decide that @fig-qq is evidence for or against the assumption,
justify your decision.
If you decide that @fig-qq provides no information about the assumption,
state what would be informative instead.


### Part (a)

(2 points)
$E(\epsilon_i|X_1,\dotsc,X_n) = 0$

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

@fig-qq provides no information.
To evaluate this assumption, we need a plot of the residuals as a function
of the explanatory variable.

Note: a plot of the residuals against $X$ (such as a scatter plot of the residuals) would be needed. Saying "scatter plot" or "residual plot" alone would not be sufficient.

:::

### Part (b)

(2 points)
The observations are iid.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

@fig-qq provides no information.
Instead, we would need to examine how the data were collected.

:::

### Part (c)

(2 points)
$Var(\epsilon_i|X_1,\dotsc,X_n) = \sigma^2$

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

@fig-qq provides no information.
Instead, we would need a plot of the residuals as a function
of the explanatory variable.
        
Note: same as (a)

:::

### Part (d)

(2 points)
$\epsilon_i|X_1,\dotsc,X_n$ is normally distributed.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

@fig-qq is evidence against the validity of this assumption
in this data set.
We know this because the points deviate strongly from the reference line.

:::

## Problem 3

(4 points)
Suppose you and your colleagues agree that the following assumptions are met for 
a simple linear regression that you've run:

- $E(\epsilon_i|X_1,\dotsc,X_n) = 0$
- The observations are iid.
- $Var(\epsilon_i|X_1,\dotsc,X_n) = \sigma^2$

Without any additional information,
which of the following claims can you make?
Select all that apply.

(a) We can interpret the coefficients.
(b) The standard errors are accurate.
(c) If we increase our sample size, our estimators will get close to the true values.
(d) We can interpret the p-values generated by R.


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

(a), (b), and (c)

    
:::
